A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ControlSpeech. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech-synthesis evaluations and ablations, including style control, unseen-speaker cloning, and mixture/noise experiments in Tables 1–6.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations and ablations in Tables 1–7, plus an SMSD representation analysis in Appendix B and Figure 3.

M1.justification: The main architecture, SMSD components, inference procedure, and loss equations remain. However, v2 changes Equation 2 from addition to concatenation and introduces KL-divergence training prose without revising the stated objective. The PDFs do not resolve whether these are corrections and explanations or actual procedural changes.

E1.justification: Both use TextrolSpeech-derived VccmDataset for main style control, unseen-speaker cloning, unseen-style descriptions, and many-to-many control. v2's test sets A–D correspond to existing groups; the new visualization analyzes existing style attributes rather than introducing another dataset or task.

E2.justification: PromptTTS 2 replaces PromptTTS in the style-control comparisons in Tables 1 and 3. Salle, PromptStyle, and InstructTTS remain, as do VALL-E and MobileSpeech in the cloning comparison. Newly discussed AudioBox is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: WER transcription changes from Whisper3 in v1 Section 4.1 to CTC-based HuBERT in v2 Appendix E, limiting direct comparison of WER values. The new t-SNE analysis uses 1,000 descriptions per attribute setting with other factors controlled. Existing test-set sizes and the 30-sample, at-least-10-listener subjective protocol remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds t-SNE analysis of SMSD style separation and distribution spread. It removes v1's ground-truth-versus-prompt timbre sensitivity finding and the qualitative account of unsuccessful FACodec modifications. The existing decoupling, SMSD, mixture-count, and noise-mode ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 1 newly defines the reported ± quantities as standard deviations; v1 leaves them undefined. Neither version specifies training seed counts or formal significance tests. Changed uncertainty values elsewhere do not establish additional runs or a changed estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Results change throughout the matched tables. ControlSpeech's Table 1 pitch accuracy changes from 0.713 to 0.833 and MOS-Q from 3.85 to 3.91; Table 3 changes PromptStyle's MOS-Q from 4.65 to 3.65. Table 1 WER changes from 4.2 to 2.9 under a different ASR evaluator, so this is not a same-setting gain. The relocated non-decoupled ablation loses WER, Spk-sv, and MOS-Q entries. Revised noise-mode results make isotropic-across-clusters best on both reported metrics, whereas v1's isotropic mode had higher diversity.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2 remove the subtractive style expression and replace codec addition with explicit concatenation. The definition of T is corrected to the duration-expanded text length. The Gaussian-mixture formulation and SMSD loss derivation, including Equation 10, remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The central simultaneous zero-shot cloning/style-control claim and SMSD contribution remain. v2 explicitly claims priority for identifying and analyzing the many-to-many problem, whereas v1 reports discovering it without that explicit first-work claim. The reorganized contribution categories mostly restate existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 removes the codec-optimization and restricted-style-description limitations from v1 Appendix H, alongside the FACodec explanation for poorer WER. It newly attributes out-of-domain generalization to SMSD, interprets t-SNE spread as diversity, and claims smaller degradation on all metrics than baselines. An ethics statement adds voice-spoofing risks and proposed mitigations. These substantially revise the account of mechanisms, limitations, and applicability.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies six decoder layers and a convolutional/LSTM style extractor producing a 512-dimensional vector. It clarifies ablation implementations, cloning-baseline training data, and the ASR checkpoint. Toolkit documentation adds weights and interfaces, but shifts from already-open-sourced wording to a planned release despite retaining availability language elsewhere; actual availability remains unresolved from the PDFs.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the codec survey, adding works such as HILCodec, RepCodec, Single-Codec, and WavTokenizer, and introduces an AudioBox comparison. Section 3.3 repositions PromptTTS 2: v1 acknowledges a related one-to-many issue, while v2 argues its missing-timbre problem is fundamentally different from ControlSpeech's within-style variation problem.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and method explanations are extensively rewritten. v2 subdivides codec decoupling/generation, consolidates experimental findings into Section 4.2, reorganizes the appendices, moves metric details out of the main text, and adds an ethics section. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 2 revises module labels and mixture-component graphics, and Figure 3 adds three t-SNE panels. The existing decoupling comparison moves from Table 1 into a narrower Table 5. Captions and energy/volume headings are revised, while the overall page template and most table structures remain.

improvement.justification: v2 improves exposition and implementation disclosure and adds a newer baseline and SMSD visualization. However, it removes the reported 5–10% degradation with prompt timbre and substantive limitations, reducing disclosure of failure conditions. Its new claim of smaller degradation on all metrics also exceeds Tables 1 and 3: pitch accuracy drops 0.083 for ControlSpeech versus 0.061 for PromptStyle. These competing gains in clarity and evidence and losses in qualification and transparency prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
